explanations.explanation: I get it, friend, because that's exactly how it works with me. If you're not standing right next to my oven, I have NO idea what you're thinking. But David tells the LORD in Psalm 139:2, "You understand my thoughts from afar." Distance doesn't slow the LORD down one bit.

You caught it, friend. In Psalm 139:2, David tells the LORD, "You understand my thoughts from afar." Close up, far away, it makes no difference to Him. Me, I lose track of my own thoughts from across the bakery.

ALL of them, friend, not a single one left out. The LORD searches out David's path and his lying down, and then David says in Psalm 139:3, "You are aware of all my ways." Walking, resting, everything in between. I'm aware of maybe three of my ways, and one of them is losing my timer.

Some would already be impressive, friend, I'll give you that. But David goes all the way. He tells the LORD in Psalm 139:3, "You are aware of all my ways." Not a sample batch, not a handful, the WHOLE tray.
Most, friend? So close it hurts. Most is how I describe my good batches. David tells the LORD in Psalm 139:3, "You are aware of all my ways." The LORD doesn't have a "mostly" setting.

explanations.answer: Before a word is on his tongue
explanations.explanation: BEFORE, friend! David says in Psalm 139:4, "Even before a word is on my tongue, You know all about it, O LORD." The word hasn't even shown up yet and the LORD already knows all about it. Meanwhile I find out what I'm saying about the same time everybody else does.

That's how the rest of us find out, friend. Somebody talks, then we know. But the LORD is way earlier than that. David says in Psalm 139:4, "Even before a word is on my tongue, You know all about it, O LORD."

Writing it down? Friend, the LORD doesn't need a screenshot from the group chat. David says in Psalm 139:4 that even before a word is on his tongue, the LORD knows all about it. Before it's said, before it's typed, before ANYTHING. I write my cookie recipes down and STILL forget them.

explanations.answer: It's too wonderful for him to reach
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. David says in Psalm 139:6, "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me, too lofty for me to attain." I picture the man just standing there, looking up, speechless. Same, David, same. I've been baking for ages and I still can't explain how my oven knows when to beep.

explanations.answer: It's easy enough for him to explain
explanations.explanation: Easy? Friend, David throws his hands up on this one. In Psalm 139:6 he says, "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me, too lofty for me to attain." Too high to reach. Picture me trying to grab the top shelf of the bakery with a mustache that only stretches so far.

explanations.answer: It's something he figured out long ago
explanations.explanation: Long ago? He hasn't figured it out at ALL, friend, and he says so. In Psalm 139:6, David calls this knowledge "too wonderful for me, too lofty for me to attain." That's not a man with it all worked out. That's a man looking up and going, WOW.

Sheol sure sounds like a good spot to be left alone, friend. But David says in Psalm 139:8, "If I ascend to the heavens, You are there; if I make my bed in Sheol, You are there." The heavens or Sheol, same answer both times. Wherever David makes his bed, the LORD is there.

Exactly, friend, no alone time in Sheol either. David says in Psalm 139:8, "If I ascend to the heavens, You are there; if I make my bed in Sheol, You are there." Two places, and both times he says, You are there. Believe me, I tried the back of a drawer for years, and I got found anyway.

explanations.answer: Guide him and hold him fast
explanations.explanation: You got it, friend. David says in Psalm 139:10, "even there Your hand will guide me; Your right hand will hold me fast." The farthest sea, and the LORD's hand is still right on him. That's a GRIP. I can't even hold onto a cookie box when somebody sneezes.

No shove back to the shore here, friend. David says in Psalm 139:10, "even there Your hand will guide me; Your right hand will hold me fast." Right there, way out by the farthest sea, the LORD guides him and holds on. Nobody gets pushed anywhere.

explanations.answer: Let go and let him wander
explanations.explanation: Let go? Friend, it's the total opposite. In Psalm 139:10 David says, "Your right hand will hold me fast." Way out by the farthest sea, that hand guides him and holds on tight. Think of me with a fresh tray of cookies. I am NOT letting go.

TRUE, friend. In Psalm 139:12, David says "even the darkness is not dark to You" and that settles it. The hiding spot he just pictured doesn't hide a thing. Me, I turned off the bakery lights once to sneak a cookie and walked face first into the oven.

I hear you, friend, dark usually means hidden. That's why I do all my secret cookie taste tests with the lights off. But in Psalm 139:12, David says "even the darkness is not dark to You" about the LORD. The darkness David pictured hiding him doesn't hide a thing from Him.

He PRAISES, friend. David says in Psalm 139:14, "I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." He thinks about how the LORD knit him together and goes straight to praise. When I look back at my early stamps, praise is NOT the first word that comes out.
Asking why is a very human move, friend. I ask my oven why every single morning. But David goes another way here. He says in Psalm 139:14, "I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made."

Quiet? Not David, friend. In Psalm 139:14 he tells the LORD straight up, "I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." The man put it in a psalm for the choirmaster, no less (Psalm 139:1). That's the opposite of keeping it to yourself.

Made in secret sure sounds hidden, friend, I'll give you that. But David says in Psalm 139:15, "My frame was not hidden from You when I was made in secret, when I was woven together in the depths of the earth." Secret to everybody else, but not to the LORD. Every bit of David's frame was in plain view for Him.

Right on, friend. David tells the LORD in Psalm 139:15 that his frame "was not hidden from You" even while he was made in secret and woven together in the depths of the earth. Secret, deep down, and STILL not hidden. Meanwhile I hide one cookie behind the cookie boxes and can't find it myself the next day.

BEFORE, friend. David says in Psalm 139:16, "all my days were written in Your book and ordained for me before one of them came to be." Not one day had happened yet, and they were already written. I can't even plan tomorrow's batch until I've hit snooze twice.

After would make the LORD a great record keeper, friend, but David goes way earlier than that. In Psalm 139:16 he says his days were "written in Your book and ordained for me before one of them came to be." Written ahead of time, every one of them. Not a diary, friend, a plan.

Once is close, friend, but David reaches back even further. In Psalm 139:16 he says his days were ordained for him "before one of them came to be." Before day one, they were already in the LORD's book. That's like having the whole cookie box packed before I've stamped a single cookie.

More time sounds like it would do the trick, friend. But David tells God in Psalm 139:18, "If I were to count them, they would outnumber the grains of sand" and that's not a time problem. That's a sand problem. I tried counting the sprinkles in one jar and quit before noon.

That's it, friend. David tells God in Psalm 139:18, "If I were to count them, they would outnumber the grains of sand" so no clock in the world fixes that. I lose count of the chocolate chips in ONE batch. He's talking about SAND.

That's the one, friend. David says to God in Psalm 139:20 that they "speak of You deceitfully; Your enemies take Your name in vain." He calls them God's enemies, people who misuse God's own name. It's a heavy turn in the psalm, and David doesn't soften it.

Old friends? There's no history like that in these verses, friend. David says to God in Psalm 139:20, "Your enemies take Your name in vain." He describes them as God's enemies who speak of God deceitfully. Nothing about a falling out over a borrowed cookie box.

I can see why soldiers came to mind, friend, with all that talk of bloodthirsty men. But David never says where they're from. In Psalm 139:20 he calls them God's enemies, people who "speak of You deceitfully" and who take God's name in vain. What he points to is how they treat God's name.

explanations.answer: He hates them as his enemies
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend, David answers his own question straight. In Psalm 139:22 he says, "I hate them with perfect hatred; I count them as my enemies." The people who hate the LORD, David counts as his own enemies. It's a raw, honest line, and he doesn't dress it up.

Not in this line, friend. Here David says in Psalm 139:22, "I hate them with perfect hatred; I count them as my enemies." He's honest with the LORD about exactly where he stands. He counts the people who hate the LORD as his own enemies.

Pity would be gentler, friend, but David doesn't go there. In Psalm 139:22 he says, "I hate them with perfect hatred; I count them as my enemies." Strong words, said plainly to the LORD. David isn't hiding anything in this prayer, not even the hard stuff.

TRUE, friend. In Psalm 139:23 David prays, "Search me, O God, and know my heart" and he means it. He's inviting the search himself. I won't even let anybody peek in my oven early, and David is opening up his whole heart.

He really does ask, friend, and that's the twist. In Psalm 139:23 David prays, "Search me, O God, and know my heart" right after all that talk about God's enemies. Most of us would hide the messy parts, like me stuffing my crooked early stamps behind the takeout menus. David says, come look.

LEAD, friend. David ends the psalm praying in Psalm 139:24, "See if there is any offensive way in me; lead me in the way everlasting." First he asks God to look, then he asks God to lead. He's not asking for a map, friend. He's asking for a Guide.

Leave looks a lot like lead, friend, but they go in opposite directions. David prays in Psalm 139:24, "lead me in the way everlasting." This whole psalm is about a God David can't get away from, and David asks Him to lead. I know a thing or two about getting left in a drawer, and trust me, lead is the one you want.

Hide, friend? David spent a big chunk of this psalm finding out there's no hiding from the LORD. So at the end he prays in Psalm 139:24, "lead me in the way everlasting." No hiding spot, just a Guide. Honestly, after years behind the takeout menus, I'd pick being led too.
